edits.after: PEC illustrates the competing effect of sampling overhead in Section~\ref{sec:pec_signature}. Here an effective-shot proxy samples the ideal multinomial distribution with $n_{\rm eff}=\lfloor B/\gamma^2\rfloor$ shots per candidate, giving covariance $\Sigma_{\rm ideal}/n_{\rm eff}$ for ideal single-shot covariance $\Sigma_{\rm ideal}$. This calculation models the overhead without sampling signed circuit contributions. The aggregate inequalities $\MSE_{\PEC}<\MSE_{\Raw}$ and $\GRI_{\PEC}>\GRI_{\Raw}$ hold at budgets $768,1536,3072,6144$. Both inequalities hold on $5/8,7/8,7/8,7/8$ instances, respectively. The observed separation therefore depends on both the landscape and the overhead. These budgets cover evaluation; they exclude the cost of learning a physical correction.

edits.after: To examine sensitivity to the noise model, a heterogeneous-PEC Gaussian proxy uses the ideal mean and covariance $\gamma^2\Sigma_{\Raw}$, with overhead $\gamma^2=88.94$. Its GRI exceeds Raw's throughout the evaluated budgets. This proxy scales noisy covariance, whereas Fig.~\ref{fig:accuracy_decision_separation} uses ideal multinomial samples. Under amplitude damping plus phase damping, a separate calculation uses known moments and $B$ shots per candidate and scale: Raw costs $B$ and ZNE costs $3B$. The analytic decision-aware prediction beats Raw on $0/16$ instances at every budget, so the planned empirical stage was not triggered. These controls identify regimes in which the available correction and its sampling cost provide no decision gain.

Covariance predictions retain the mitigation coefficients used in the executed circuits. edits.before: Covariance derivatives use Cholesky conditioning and an analytic bivariate density; the supported double-precision regime requires correlation condition number at most $10^{14}$.
edits.after: General covariance derivatives use Cholesky conditioning and an analytic bivariate density; the supported double-precision regime requires correlation condition number at most $10^{14}$. For gaps sharing one incumbent, the implementation instead evaluates the full analytic gradient by one-dimensional conditional-normal integration. Symmetric off-diagonal derivatives contribute half to each matrix entry, so Frobenius contraction gives the first-order risk change.

edits.before: Any nonpositive gap, including an exact tie, counts as failure.
edits.after: For a strict single-selection decision, any nonpositive gap, including an exact tie, counts as failure. In the dynamic search, exact estimator ties retain the first candidate within a batch and the earlier incumbent across rounds. Its success criterion is ideal regret at most $\epsilon$ relative to the best candidate visited along that trajectory; $\epsilon$ is fixed from the archived ideal landscape.
